title: Concentration–time graphs, half-life and clock reactions; Rate-determining step and mechanisms
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: KN05#t1 term and clue written for the game; KN06#t4 term and clue written for the game; KN06#t2 term and clue written for the game; KN06#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: KN05#N.11, KN06#N.3a, KN05#N.12a, KN06#N.8, KN06#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Half-life
items.clue: The time taken to lose 50% of what is left of a reactant.

items.label: Molecularity
items.clue: The number of particles that collide, or break up, in one elementary stage.

items.label: Intermediate
items.clue: Forms in one stage and is used up in a later one; it sits at an energy minimum.

items.label: Rate-determining step
items.clue: The slowest stage of a mechanism, which limits how fast the whole reaction goes.

questions.stem: In an iodine clock, the blue-black colour appears after 48 s. A second run uses double the concentration of I⁻, with everything else the same, and the colour appears after 24 s. What is the order with respect to I⁻?

options.text: Zero order, as the same amount of iodine forms in both runs.
Order −1, as the time halves when [I⁻] doubles.
Second order, as [I⁻] doubles and the time halves: a factor of 2 × 2.
First order, as 1/t doubles when [I⁻] doubles.

questions.explanation: Rate ∝ 1/t. Doubling [I⁻] doubles 1/t, so the rate is proportional to [I⁻]: first order.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a reaction intermediate from a transition state in a multistep reaction?

options.text: A transition state can be isolated if the reaction is stopped quickly enough, just as an intermediate can.
An intermediate is present at the start and is re-formed at the end; a transition state is used up.
An intermediate lies at an energy minimum between steps; a transition state is at a maximum and cannot be isolated.
An intermediate appears in the overall equation for the reaction; a transition state does not.

questions.explanation: The intermediate sits in a dip, so it lasts long enough to be detected in principle. The transition state is a peak.

questions.stem: A hypothetical compound X decomposes at constant temperature. Results: t = 0, 200, 400, 600 s; [X] = 0.640, 0.320, 0.160, 0.080 mol dm⁻³. A new run at the same temperature starts at [X] = 0.320 mol dm⁻³. How long does [X] take to fall to 0.080 mol dm⁻³?
questions.explanation: [X] halves every 200 s, whatever the start: first order. 0.320 → 0.160 → 0.080 is two halvings: 400 s.

questions.stem: The overall equation for a reaction is 2X + Y → X₂Y. The experimental rate equation is rate = k[X][Y]. Which mechanism is consistent with both?

options.text: Step 1: X + Y → XY (slow). Step 2: XY + X → X₂Y (fast).
Step 1: X + X → X₂ (slow). Step 2: X₂ + Y → X₂Y (fast).
Step 1: X + Y ⇌ XY (fast). Step 2: XY + X → X₂Y (slow).
Step 1: X + Y → XY (slow). Step 2: XY + Y → XY₂ (fast).

questions.explanation: The steps add to 2X + Y → X₂Y, and the slow first step has one X and one Y: rate = k[X][Y].

questions.stem: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is hydrolysed by aqueous sodium hydroxide. Its rate equation is rate = k[(CH₃)₃CCl]. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The mechanism is SN2: OH⁻ attacks the carbon as the C–Cl bond breaks, in one step.
The mechanism is SN1: the slow step forms a carbocation; OH⁻ reacts later, in a fast step.
The mechanism is SN1: OH⁻ and (CH₃)₃CCl react together in the slow step, which is unimolecular.
The mechanism is SN2, as tertiary halogenoalkanes react through one transition state.

questions.explanation: Only (CH₃)₃CCl is in the slow step, so OH⁻ must react after it: SN1.
